title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed all planned pairs (complete_pair_count = 200) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design and execution accounting, summarize independent emulator corroboration on a 10% holdout (20 tasks) that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements, and discuss operational implications and threats to validity. Preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises productivity gains for network operators but introduces risk: generated device commands can be syntactically incorrect, violate workflow constraints (e.g., make‑before‑break), or cause outages. Prior work therefore advocates grounding LLM outputs with deterministic checkers and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) or with constrained agent architectures to reduce such risks. However, the practical marginal benefit of automated repair depends on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under a chosen generator/prompting policy, (ii) validator coverage and fidelity, and (iii) the repair budget and repair effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question and executed a paired experiment designed to isolate the marginal effect of invoking a deterministic validator and a single repair attempt on the identical initial LLM output. Research question: Does a deterministic GVR pipeline materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? Contributions: (1) a sealed preregistered paired experiment (n=200) comparing LLM‑only vs GVR under shared‑initial semantics; (2) artifact‑grounded result accounting showing zero baseline validator failures under the chosen generation policy and associated statistical inference; (3) a discussion of methodological tradeoffs and recommendations for operational evaluation and guardrail design.
sections.related_work: Empirical studies and surveys show that large language models make factual errors and that mitigation approaches include retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, constrained generation, and agent guardrails. NetOps prototypes demonstrate the feasibility of intent→configuration translation but typically lack externally auditable, production‑like failure‑rate measurements. Architectural proposals recommend combining LLM generators with deterministic validators (Batfish‑style or vendor‑aware checkers) and with emulator/testbed verification; red‑team audits document configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that can alter safety outcomes. Our study situates itself as an externally archived, preregistered measurement that isolates the marginal effect of deterministic repair for a fixed model and a fixed shared‑initial sampling policy.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The preregistered experiment (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one deterministic shared initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the primary test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs were computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729).

Task bank and validators. The task bank comprised 200 machine‑checkable intent→configuration tasks balanced across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge). Each task encodes initial and expected final state plus workflow constraints (e.g., make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields). The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces syntax and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as an independent disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator blind spots at the data‑plane level; any validator–emulator mismatch would be flagged and deterministically excluded from the primary analysis per the preregistered contamination plan.

Adapter semantics and sampling determinism. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task a single initial candidate was generated and reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions to obtain a paired causal contrast. The model configuration artifact records the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and a null temperature field; determinism in the paired comparison was achieved by adapter‑level reuse of the single shared generation rather than by relying on an explicit model temperature parameter. This enforcement is evidenced by the adapter accounting fields (hosted_model_call_event_count and stage counts) and by the deterministic reconciliation artifact that records a single shared_initial_generation per task and no cross‑condition re‑sampling. Those canonical artifacts are archived with the execution bundle (see canonical artifact pointers below). We therefore state precisely: runtime determinism for the paired estimand was produced by adapter‑level shared‑initial reuse (adapter audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; stage_counts indicate shared_initial_generation = 200), not by a model temperature override in the model configuration.

Analysis and handling rules. The preplanned primary test is an exact McNemar two‑sided test on the 2×2 paired table; a paired bootstrap produced percentile CIs (10,000 resamples). Missingness and exclusion rules were applied deterministically per preregistration: pairs affected by infrastructure execution failures or flagged for validator–emulator disagreement would be excluded from the primary analysis (and logged). All decision rules and seeds used for the bootstrap are recorded in the archived analysis artifacts.

Reproducibility note (documented limitation). The Mininet 10% holdout executed as preregistered and produced a contamination summary; however, the labeled archive does not include an explicit artifact naming the randomized selection seed used to draw that 10% holdout. Consequently, exact bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of which tasks comprised the holdout draw is not possible from the labeled artifacts, and we report this as a reproducibility limitation that affects reconstruction of the holdout draw (not the contamination summary value itself).
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run executed under the frozen preregistered plan and completed all planned episodes. Accounting: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), maximum_model_calls = 400, repair_calls_used = 0. Adapter audit records hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming enforced shared‑initial semantics.

Validator outcomes and inferential statistics. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Under the preregistered estimand the observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided test: p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because baseline validator failures were absent in this sample, the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis requiring a ≥50% relative reduction could not be meaningfully evaluated.

Repair branch and contamination check. No validator failures were observed; consequently, the preregistered automated repair branch was never invoked and secondary estimands (repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failures, model‑call cost per repair) have no empirical data in this run. The Mininet holdout (20 tasks) reported zero validator–emulator disagreements in the contamination summary produced by the run. As noted above, the archived contamination summary reports zero disagreements but the explicit seed for the holdout draw is not labeled in the archive, limiting exact reconstruction of the draw.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The null outcome (zero baseline validator failures) is an artifact‑grounded empirical fact for this generator/prompt policy and task bank under shared_initial semantics; it does not generalize automatically to other generators, sampling policies, models, or more adversarial task distributions. The paired shared‑initial design intentionally isolates the marginal effect of invoking a validator and a single repair on the identical candidate; this internal control excludes benefits obtainable by multi‑sample generation or nonzero‑temperature sampling that could expose failing candidates for repair.

Why the null occurred. Representative validator traces show that generated sequences satisfied required_command_count and task constraints across difficulty labels (medium, hard, very_hard), indicating the generator/prompt combination produced correct, machine‑checkable sequences for this curated bank. Adapter accounting and deterministic reconciliation confirm single shared initial calls per task, which prevented sampling variance from producing additional (possibly failing) candidates.

Operational implications. Before adopting automated repair as a primary safety investment, practitioners should (1) measure baseline validator failure prevalence under the intended generation policy on representative workloads; (2) expand validator fidelity and emulator/testbed coverage to detect validator blind spots; and (3) consider multi‑sample or ensemble generation and larger repair budgets when baseline failures are nontrivial. When baseline validator failures are rare, single‑step automated repair yields limited marginal returns for validator‑detected errors; resources may be better directed toward richer validators, larger emulation sampling, or adversarial testing.

Methodological tradeoffs and next steps. A paired shared‑initial design provides a clear causal contrast but underestimates unconditional operational failure risk that arises from sampling variability. Future preregistered runs should include mixed designs with per‑condition multi‑sample draws, larger repair budgets (multi‑step repairs or human‑in‑the‑loop escalation), broader emulator coverage, and multiple models to probe model‑dependent brittleness. The archival artifacts from this run provide canonical examples of validator traces, adapter accounting, and paired contingency outputs to guide such extensions.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. This artifact‑grounded outcome emphasizes that GVR’s marginal utility depends on workload and baseline failure prevalence; operational assurance should therefore prioritize representative baseline measurement and validator fidelity before relying on single‑step automated repair as a primary mitigation.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: orchestration used hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Deterministic paired semantics: runtime determinism for the paired estimand was achieved by adapter‑level shared_initial reuse (adapter audit records a single shared_initial_generation per task and hosted_model_call_event_count = 200), not by reliance on a model temperature override in the model configuration (the model configuration artifact contains a null temperature field). Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan (start: 2026‑08‑30T11:50:34.530059Z; end: 2026‑08‑30T12:12:07.541650Z); model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Mininet holdout: a Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered and executed on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) as an independent contamination detector; the run produced zero validator–emulator disagreements for that holdout in the contamination summary. Reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet 10% holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive; this absence prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the drawn holdout despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. No post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (adapter accounting records a single shared initial invocation per task). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
